Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

vignette: Dr. Minh Pham, a 51-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and dentist, had experienced severe psychological distress following a traumatic stalking incident that occurred several years ago. Dr. Pham had always taken pride in her meticulous attention to detail and her ability to handle stressful situations with calm professionalism. However, the trauma she faced shattered her sense of safety and security. The incident began when a former patient became obsessed with her, sending multiple threatening messages and showing up unannounced at both her home and workplace. Dr. Pham’s husband had been supportive throughout this ordeal, but despite his reassurances and the presence of police officers who were assigned to patrol near her residence, she found it nearly impossible to believe that she was truly safe. Since then, certain songs that reminded her of the stalking period would trigger intense anxiety and flashbacks. Dr. Pham recalled one particular day when a song played on the radio during her commute; she immediately felt her heart racing as memories flooded back, causing her to pull over and sit in silence until the panic subsided. Exposure to any media content related to stalking or similar incidents would also trigger her symptoms. She had started avoiding watching television shows or reading news articles that might remind her of the traumatic event. Even though she knew logically that these triggers were not directly dangerous, they elicited a visceral reaction that made it difficult for her to function normally. The presence of authority figures like police officers, who initially provided some comfort, now reminded Dr. Pham of the stalking incident and its ongoing threat. She found herself feeling anxious around them, even though she knew their presence was meant to protect her. Dr. Pham’s sense of safety had become deeply compromised. Even in environments where others told her she was safe, like at home or at work, she could not shake off the feeling of vulnerability. This led her to adopt specific behaviors that she believed would make her feel more secure. She always chose seating arrangements based on how well she could see and control her surroundings. At work, she insisted on having a chair that faced away from patients so she could monitor the room at all times. The need for complete visibility was paramount; she felt unsafe unless her back was against a wall where she could have a clear view of everything around her. This behavior extended to her personal life as well—she always positioned herself in social gatherings with her back to a wall, which made it difficult to fully engage with friends and family. Over time, these avoidance behaviors began to impact her professional and personal relationships. At work, she found herself increasingly isolated from colleagues because of her need for constant vigilance. Her husband noticed that she was withdrawing from social activities they once enjoyed together, and this had created tension in their relationship. What frightened Dr. Pham most was the fear that she would never fully feel safe again. She worried about how these symptoms were affecting not only her life but also her ability to provide care for her patients with the same level of dedication and focus she once did. Despite these challenges, she was determined to regain control over her life. It was a particularly distressing day when one of her favorite songs came on at work, causing an intense panic attack that left her unable to see any more patients for the rest of the day. This incident finally convinced Dr. Pham that she needed help to manage these symptoms and reclaim her sense of safety. She began seeking therapy, hoping to find ways to cope with her triggers and regain a semblance of normalcy in both her personal and professional life. Dr. Pham was cautiously optimistic about her future, hoping that through therapy she could learn strategies to mitigate the impact of her traumatic experiences and eventually lead a more fulfilling life without being constantly on guard.
